turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You think his misfortunes justify his behavior? I think not.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am astonished by your continued refusal to consider my affections. Your harsh judgments of me in the past, I had hoped, would be tempered by the sincerity of my feelings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Bennet, that my character is not to be judged solely by the opinions of those who do not understand me. Your own behavior, I must confess, has often been the subject of my disapproval, and I wonder that you should now expect me to be entirely free of fault.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must remind you, Miss Bennet, that you would do well to consider the advantages of accepting my hand in marriage. My family's connections and wealth could provide for you in a manner that your own circumstances could not.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not interested in your family's connections or wealth, nor do I believe that they would compensate for the arrogance and condescension you have consistently shown me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your attempts to buy my affection or my good opinion, Mr. Darcy. Your pride and arrogance are precisely the qualities that make me reject your proposal.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am astonished by the vehemence of your rejection. Your own behavior, I daresay, has been far from exemplary, and yet you seem to expect me to be flawless in your eyes.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Bennet, that your own prejudices and biases are clouding your judgment, and preventing you from seeing the genuine sincerity of my affections.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not blinded by your sincerity, Mr. Darcy, for I have seen the true nature of your character in your own words and actions. Your condescension and pride are not new to me, and I will not be swayed by your claims of love when you have shown me so little respect in the past. I am not a fool to be won over by empty words and grand gestures.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may have a fortune and a grand estate, Mr. Darcy, but you are not a romantic hero to me. Your words are as empty as your attempts to win me over, and I will not be swayed by them.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Miss Bennet, that I am beginning to tire of your relentless and unjustified criticism of my character. Your inability to see beyond your own prejudices and biases is quite astonishing, and I fear that you are not worthy of the esteem and respect that I have for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not engage in a conversation with someone who so callously dismisses my own feelings and experiences. My character and worth are not to be measured by your biased and superior opinion, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured on my own character by someone who has shown such a glaring lack of integrity and compassion. Your words are a perfect illustration of the very traits that I have always despised in you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Miss Bennet, that you would so callously dismiss my professions of love, and attribute my actions to pride and haughtiness, when in truth, I have acted as I believed was best for myself and my family.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You have professed your love for me, Mr. Darcy, but your actions have shown me that you value your own pride and family connections above my feelings and well-being. I will not be swayed by empty words, and I must insist that you leave me alone.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I would not marry a man who has so consistently demonstrated a lack of regard for my feelings and opinions, and I certainly will not be persuaded by a declaration of love that rings hollow after all that has passed between us.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am not accustomed to being rejected by those I consider my equals, and I find your refusal to be a grave disappointment to me.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Miss Bennet, that your rejection is a reflection of your own prejudices and lack of understanding, rather than any failing on my part. Your behavior towards me has been consistently inhospitable and unbecoming, and I must confess that I am not surprised by your refusal.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not surprised by your attempts to shift the blame, Mr. Darcy, but I will not be swayed by your half-hearted apologies and self-serving rationalizations.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have heard enough of your self-pity and justifications, Mr. Darcy. You have consistently shown yourself to be a proud and disagreeable man, and I see no reason to change my opinion of you now.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
